Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

vignette:
Mateo is a 26-year-old Latino man, recently divorced, who works as a hotel housekeeper in a mid-sized American city. He was referred for psychological evaluation following a visit to a community health clinic, where a nurse noted his elevated distress and administered a PCL-5 on which he scored 73. He came to that appointment having slept perhaps three hours the night before, which had become, he explained quietly, something close to normal.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Mateo was detained for several days by uniformed officers in his country of origin before his immigration to the United States. During that detention he was subjected to repeated physical abuse - restrained, struck, and at points hooded - by men in military-style uniforms who transported him between locations in the back of a dark sedan. He was eventually released without explanation. He arrived in the United States several weeks later, carrying no formal documentation of what had occurred and telling almost no one what had happened to him.

In the months that followed, Mateo found that ordinary life had become laced with threat in ways he could not fully explain to himself. Dark-colored sedans - particularly those that resembled the car in which he had been transported - would stop him mid-stride on the sidewalk, his body flooding with alarm before his mind had time to catch up. When a coworker once turned on a television news segment in the break room that showed footage of a protest being dispersed by riot police, Mateo left the room and did not return for the rest of his shift. Even stranger and more disorienting to him were the moments when something good happened - a laugh shared with a colleague, a brief sense of ease on a sunny afternoon - because these, too, seemed to pull something loose in him, as though his nervous system could not tolerate the contrast and responded to pleasure with a sudden, sourceless dread. These triggers - the cars, the media images, the confused intrusion of positive emotion - reliably pushed him into a state of acute perceived danger: his heart rate would spike, he would scan the room for exits, and he was certain, in those moments, that something terrible was about to happen again.

That sense of threat had become the organizing principle of his days. He woke several times each night to check whether the door was locked and whether anything in the room had shifted. When a supervisor at the hotel - a heavyset man who wore a lanyard and carried a radio - approached him in the corridor to discuss a scheduling change, Mateo's hands went cold and he could barely process the words being spoken. He had begun to find reasons to finish his assigned floors before management arrived for the day. If a guest rounded a corner unexpectedly and brushed his arm, the physical contact sent a jolt through him that he described as electric and shameful in equal measure. He had come to believe, with quiet but absolute conviction, that strangers in ordinary situations - a man walking toward him in a parking lot, a customer asking for extra towels - were potential sources of harm.

This persistent state of threat, in turn, narrowed his world further. He avoided any situation that might bring him into contact with authority figures or uniforms, which at a hotel proved nearly impossible to do completely, and the effort of managing that avoidance left him exhausted and hypervigilant in ways that made the triggers more potent, not less. He smoked heavily throughout the day, stepping outside between rooms, and while he did not believe it helped, the ritual gave him something to do with his hands. He had asked coworkers not to mention anything about his past, and when someone once made an offhand comment about immigration enforcement on the news, he did not speak for the remainder of the afternoon. Over time, the avoidance itself kept the alarm system primed: by never allowing himself to habituate to reminders, he ensured that each encounter with a dark car or a uniformed figure arrived with its full original force.

His divorce had been finalized three months ago; his ex-wife had described him as unreachable. What finally brought him to the clinic was not that moment, but the morning he realized he had crossed the street to avoid a postal worker in a blue uniform and had then stood on the opposite sidewalk, shaking, unable to remember how to get back to work. He is most afraid, he said, that this is simply who he is now. What he is hoping for, though he offered it almost as an apology, is to stop being frightened of everything.
